---
title: "Outcomes and decision evidence"
subtitle: "Burden estimates that answer a program question"
---

Programs ask a narrower question than papers do. They want to know how large a problem is in their own population, which subgroup carries most of it, and whether a change is real or is an artifact of reporting. I build burden and outcome tables from public data to answer that question directly, and I write the assumptions next to the numbers so that a reader can see which conclusions survive a different assumption. My MBA and my work in state government mean I am comfortable with the fact that the answer has to fit on one page and inform a decision that is being made anyway.

## Artifacts

**Burden table from public data.** Counts, rates, and a subgroup breakdown for a defined condition and population, built from an open source with the extraction code published. Denominator choice, suppression rule, and confidence interval method stated in the table footnotes.

**Briefing note.** One page showing how a burden estimate was framed for a non-technical audience and what the program did with it.

*Both of those artifacts are in preparation.*

**Usual sleep and frequent mental distress, BRFSS 2022.** A prespecified cross-sectional analysis of the public CDC file: the weighted prevalence of 14 or more poor mental health days among adults who report under 7 hours of sleep, compared with adults who report 7 to 9 hours, in the 50 states and the District of Columbia. The [protocol](../notebooks/brfss-2022-sleep-fmd/protocol.qmd), the [analysis plan](../notebooks/brfss-2022-sleep-fmd/sap.qmd), and the [case study](../notebooks/brfss-2022-sleep-fmd/case-study.qmd) are the record. This is independent sample work on a public survey. It is not a Nebraska DHHS product, not a pharmaceutical or regulatory submission, and not an analysis of a commercial claims database.

## What I actually did

- Burden and trend analyses supporting state overdose, injury, and suicide prevention programs.
- Program reporting products for CDC, BJA, and NHTSA funded programs, aimed at program staff rather than at reviewers.
- Dashboards and recurring reports in Power BI and Tableau built on surveillance data.
- Health economics coursework and an MBA, applied to framing and communication rather than to formal modeling.

## What I am not claiming

::: {.limits}
This is not market access work. I have not written an AMCP dossier, a global value dossier, or an HTA submission, and I do not build cost-effectiveness or budget impact models in TreeAge or equivalent tools. Where a role needs that, my contribution is the epidemiology input, meaning burden, natural history, and comparator selection, not ownership of the economic model.
:::
